items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] Auto-detect the failed layer with the nozzle force sensor and resume (A1 / A1M)
items.content_html:
Problem
When filament stops feeding mid-print (clog, tangle, grinding), the printer keeps “printing” in the air. By the time you notice, the nozzle is several mm above the part and hours of printing are wasted. Resuming is possible in principle, but the hardest part is finding the exact layer where it failed. Measuring the part with calipers is slow and error-prone.

Proposal

  1. Add a “Resume from failure” function. With the failed part still on the bed, the printer probes several points on top of it with a cold nozzle, using the force sensor that the A1 series already uses for bed leveling. The slicer knows the model geometry, so it picks the probe points.
  2. From the measured heights the printer determines the last successfully printed layer.
  3. The printer offers: “Print stopped at layer N (Z = X mm). Resume from here?” and continues on the same part.

Optional: detect extrusion loss during printing (force sensor + filament motion data), pause automatically, and offer the same resume, so the part is still in good shape.

Why
It saves long prints and material, and it uses hardware the A1 / A1 mini already have.

Demand

  • The general request “Resume from Layer”: Feature Request: Resume from Layer
  • A community tool that already does manual resume, Layer Rescue: Layer Rescue: resume failed prints from any layer, even after a power loss

People clearly want this. Automatic layer detection would make it safe and easy for everyone.

items.title: [thenews.com.pk] Battlefield use of AI weapons grows as Geneva talks leave rules unsettled
items.content_html: AI-enabled weapons are in use in conflicts in Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East, while campaigners say armed drones that can independently select and strike targets have appeared in limited cases. The International Committee of the Red Cross says commanders must remain responsible for the lawful use of force. At U.N.-backed talks in Geneva, 128 countries agreed to develop an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons over the next two years, but left open whether it would be legally binding. Around 100 countries had sought binding rules; the United States, Russia and Israel opposed that push, and the consensus-based forum allowed any member to block stronger language. The process is expected to examine which systems should be prohibited and which could be regulated. Government experts are to recommend the instrument’s form, including whether it should be binding. The International Committee of the Red Cross says commanders must remain responsible for the lawful use of force, including when weapons act with little or no human oversight.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

items.title: [time.com] Ebola death toll in Congo exceeds 5,700 as response lags
items.content_html: An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has surpassed 11,700 confirmed cases and 5,700 deaths as of Nov. 19, making it the country’s largest and deadliest. Cases have also been reported in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. The Bundibugyo strain is driving the outbreak, and no approved vaccine or targeted treatment is available for it. Health workers say early cases can be difficult to identify because initial symptoms resemble those of other illnesses. Late detection, population movement and mistrust of response teams have hindered containment, while attacks on health workers and burial teams have further complicated the response. On Nov. 17, health workers in Butembo, North Kivu, escalated a month-long strike over unpaid wages and bonuses, halting even minimum service at treatment centers.

items.title: [lemonde.fr] Costa’s EU budget draft cuts regional funds for first time
items.content_html: European Council President António Costa’s revised 2028-34 budget proposal would cut EU cohesion funding for the first time, reducing regional development funding by €8 billion compared with the Irish presidency’s previous draft. The change affects a coalition of 17 southern and eastern member states, including Poland, Italy and Spain, that had opposed cuts to cohesion funding. Costa’s proposal also reduces allocations for competitiveness, defence and external action. It leaves direct farm subsidies unchanged from the previous draft, but France says the proposed Common Agricultural Policy funding still fails to guarantee farmers’ income support. The revised framework cuts €204 billion from the European Commission’s original plan. EU leaders will discuss the proposal at a special summit in Brussels on November 26-27. The European Parliament must also approve the eventual budget, and its chief budget negotiator, Siegfried Muresan, has warned that lawmakers may withhold consent over the reductions.

items.content_html: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin for about 30 minutes after an APEC welcome dinner in Shenzhen on Nov. 18, the first face-to-face meeting between Japanese and Russian leaders since 2019. Japanese sources said Takaichi called for Imai’s immediate release and urged Moscow to reverse its temporary takeover of Japan Tobacco assets in Russia. Imai was arrested in Sakhalin on Oct. 13 on suspicion of espionage. His current detention period is due to expire Dec. 12 but could be extended. Japan had protested a day earlier after suspected Russian aircraft entered its airspace. The countries also disagree over Ukraine and sovereignty over disputed islands. Russia’s Presidential Executive Office had not publicly confirmed the conversation.

items.title: [theguardian.com] EU proposes extra €45 billion Ukraine loan, faces fight over guarantees
items.content_html: The European Commission proposed on Nov. 18 an additional €45 billion loan for Ukraine in 2027, covering about two-thirds of a projected €70 billion funding gap. It would supplement the €90 billion EU loan already approved for 2026 and 2027; the new package allocates up to €25 billion for military needs and €20 billion for Ukraine’s state budget. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the funding was intended to strengthen Kyiv’s position in negotiations with Russia. Ukraine would repay the principal only after receiving Russian reparations. The EU would raise the money on capital markets, with its common budget guaranteeing the borrowing. Budget support would be conditional on Ukrainian reforms, including on the rule of law and corruption. The Commission also wants other international partners to cover the remaining €25 billion of Ukraine’s estimated needs. Approval faces resistance from Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia, which have signalled they do not want to join the financing. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pressed for all 27 EU members to share responsibility and linked the Ukraine financing to talks on the bloc’s next long-term budget; Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico called that approach “blackmail”. EU leaders are due to discuss the proposal at a Brussels summit on Nov. 26-27, and the budget guarantee requires unanimous member-state backing.
